```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 4.5)
library(fairy)
options(width = 90)
```

This vignette walks through the examples of Jekel, Regenwetter, Chen, and Line
(in preparation), *"Wait, what are you saying, exactly?" A theoretical framework
for codifying and evaluating verbal hypotheses about proportions*, and of its
online supplement, one step at a time, with the code that produces each table
and number. Every number quoted from the paper is also checked by the
package's tests (`tests/testthat/test-paper-*.R`).

The package does what "the mathematics fairy" does in the paper (it does not store the paper's models; you enter them as constraint strings, as shown below)
(<https://modeling-for-everyone.eu/posts/fairy/>):

| In the paper | In the package |
|:--|:--|
| minimal description via order constraints (H-representation) | `fairy_h()`, `fairy_constraints()` |
| minimal description via extreme cases (V-representation) | `fairy_vertices()`, `fairy_words()` |
| parsimony (volume) and the largest possible Bayes factor | `fairy_volume()`, `fairy_max_bf()`, `fairy_info()` |
| overlap, nesting, mixture models | `fairy_intersect()`, `fairy_nested()`, `fairy_mixture()`, `fairy_compare()` |
| replication models (identical, joint, substitutable) | `fairy_replicate()` |
| input files for QTest and multinomineq | `fairy_write_qtest()`, `fairy_write_multinomineq()` |

# Part 1: The cringyness study

## Verbal hypotheses become order constraints

Six probabilities describe the study. The probability that a randomly drawn
child, teen, or adult cringes at an illogical joke or at a pun gives the order
`p1, ..., p6`:

```{r labels}
lab <- c("illogical: children", "illogical: teens", "illogical: adults",
         "pun: children", "pun: teens", "pun: adults")
data.frame(parameter = paste0("p", 1:6), meaning = lab)
```

A model is a character string. Constraints are separated by `;`, chains such as
`p1 > p2 > p3` are allowed, and `<` and `<=` mean the same thing (as in the paper,
models are closed sets, so no software can tell `<` from `<=`). The package does not
come with the paper's models: you enter them yourself. Here are Models 1 to 9 as constraint
strings:

```{r model-strings}
strings <- c(
  M1 = "(p1+p4)/2 < (p2+p5)/2 < (p3+p6)/2",
  M2 = "p1 < p2 < p3; p4 < p5 < p6",
  M3 = "p1 > p2 > p3; p4 < p5 < p6; p1+p2+p3 < p4+p5+p6",
  M4 = "p1 > p2 > p3; p4 < p5 < p6; p1 < p4; p2 < p5; p3 < p6",
  M5 = "p1 = p2 = p3 = p4 = p5 = p6",
  M6 = "p1 > p2 > p3; p4 < p5 < p6; p1+p2+p3 = p4+p5+p6",
  M7 = "p1 > p2 > p3; p4 < p5 < p6; (p1+p2+p3)/3 = (p4+p5+p6)/3",
  M8 = "{p1,p2,p3,p4,p5,p6} = {p1,p2,p3,p4,p5,p6}",
  M9 = "p1 < p2 < p3; p4 > p5 > p6; p1 > p4; p2 > p5; p3 > p6"
)
```

* Model 1 is the average of the two joke types per age group, increasing with age.
* Models 7 and 8 use *approximate* equality: `approx_tol = 0.05` turns every equality into
  "within five percentage points"; it is passed to `fairy_h()` for these two models below.
* Model 10, the mixture of Models 4 and 9, is not a string: it is built with
  `fairy_mixture()` below.

```{r models}
m <- lapply(strings, fairy_h, n_p = 6)                          # H-representations of Models 1 to 9
m$M7 <- fairy_h(strings[["M7"]], n_p = 6, approx_tol = 0.05)     # approximate equalities
m$M8 <- fairy_h(strings[["M8"]], n_p = 6, approx_tol = 0.05)
m$M10 <- fairy_mixture(m$M4, m$M9)                               # the mixture of Models 4 and 9
m <- m[paste0("M", 1:10)]
names(m)
```

## Minimal descriptions via order constraints (Figure 2)

`fairy_h()` returns the non-redundant H-representation. For Model 4 the paper
reports five inequalities among pairs of parameters and two range constraints,
`0 <= p3 <= p2 <= p1 <= p4 <= p5 <= p6 <= 1`:

```{r model4-h}
fairy_constraints(m$M4)
```

The first line is the paper's `-1 x p1 + 1 x p2 <= 0`. The same constraints in the
machine-readable format of QTest are written by `fairy_write_qtest()`
(and for the R package multinomineq by `fairy_write_multinomineq()`):

```{r qtest, eval = FALSE}
fairy_write_qtest(strings["M4"], n_p = 6, file = "model4.tar")
```

The no-effect model (Model 5) is two inequalities and five equalities:

```{r model5}
fairy_info(m$M5)[, c("dim", "inequalities", "equalities", "vertices")]
```

## The mixture model (Model 10) and its 64 constraints

The mixture of Models 4 and 9 says: each person follows either Model 4 or Model 9,
with an unknown weight. Geometrically, that is the convex
hull of the two models, and `fairy_mixture()` computes its H-representation:

```{r mixture}
mix <- fairy_mixture(m$M4, m$M9)
fairy_info(mix, volume = FALSE)
```

There are 12 vertices and 64 non-redundant constraints. Twelve of them are the range constraints
`0 <= p_i <= 1`, which leaves the paper's 52 order constraints:

```{r mixture-count}
hn <- rcdd::q2d(mix)
single <- rowSums(hn[, -(1:2)] != 0) == 1
c(range = sum(single), other = sum(!single))
```

The first row of the paper's list of 52 constraints reads
`p2 <= p1 + p3 <= 1 + p2`. The package lists them too:

```{r mixture-constraints}
head(fairy_constraints(mix)[!single], 6)
```

The paper counts the "edge cases" of the vertex V1 of Table 1
(`p1 = p4 = p5 = p6 = 1`, `p2 = p3 = 0`): it satisfies 26 of the 52 order constraints with equality,
and 6 range constraints, 32 in all:

```{r edge-cases}
v1 <- c(1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1)
slack <- hn[, 2] + as.vector(hn[, -(1:2)] %*% v1)
c(order_constraints = sum(abs(slack[!single]) < 1e-9),
  range_constraints = sum(abs(slack[single]) < 1e-9),
  total = sum(abs(slack) < 1e-9))
```

## Minimal descriptions via extreme cases (Tables 1 and 2)

`fairy_words()` lists the vertices, writing a probability of 0 as "none" and of 1 as "all"
(valid for a finite population). The row order of the underlying algorithm is arbitrary,
so the rows are sorted. The labels are the six columns of the paper's tables:

```{r table1}
fairy_words(m$M4, labels = lab)       # Table 1, Model 4
```

Model 9 is the mirror image, `all` and `none` swapped:

```{r table1b}
fairy_words(m$M9, labels = lab)
```

Table 2, the 12 vertices of Model 6 (equal marginal means), contains fractions:

```{r table2}
fairy_words(m$M6, labels = lab)
```

The mixture model has the 12 vertices that are the union of those of Models 4 and 9 (the two
share the vertices "all, all, all, all, all, all" and "none, ..., none"):

```{r mixture-vertices}
nrow(fairy_vertices(m$M10))
```

Out of the 2^6 = 64 corners of the unit cube, only 12 are allowed, so the mixture model is falsifiable.

## Parsimony (Figure 3)

The parsimony of a model is its volume inside the unit cube of all conceivable families
of Binomial parameters. The inverse of the volume is the largest Bayes factor
the model can reach against the unconstrained model (uniform prior). Figure 3 of the paper
has two rectangles, their overlap and a line segment:

```{r figure3}
I   <- fairy_h("p1 < .5; p2 > .25; p2 < .75", n_p = 2)
II  <- fairy_h("p1 > .3; p1 < .7; p2 > .5", n_p = 2)
III <- fairy_intersect(I, II)
IV  <- fairy_h("p1 = .5; p2 > .25; p2 < .75", n_p = 2)

rbind(I = fairy_info(I), II = fairy_info(II), III = fairy_info(III), IV = fairy_info(IV))
```

Model I has area 0.25 (maximal Bayes factor 4), Model II 0.2 (5), their overlap
Model III 0.05 (20). Model IV contains an equality, so it is a line segment with
volume zero and **no** upper bound on the Bayes factor. The vertices of the overlap
include two new ones that are not vertices of either rectangle:

```{r figure3-vertices}
fairy_vertices(III)
```

## Model relationships (Table 3)

`fairy_compare()` returns the layout of Table 3: the diagonal gives each model's volume, entries
above the diagonal the volume of the overlap of two models, entries below the diagonal tell whether the
row model is nested in (subset sign) or contains (superset sign) the column model, and otherwise the
dimension of their overlap. The last row is the largest possible Bayes factor against the
unconstrained model.

```{r table3}
cmp <- fairy_compare(m)
cmp
```

Individual entries are available as numbers, for example the largest Bayes factor of each model
and the volume of the mixture model:

```{r table3-numbers}
round(cmp$max_bf, 1)
cmp$volume["M10", "M10"]
```

The paper reports 6, 36, 72, 720, infinity, infinity, about 200, about 10^6, 720, and about 23.
The values for Models 7 and 8 depend on the approximate-equality tolerance; with a tolerance of 0.05
the exact volumes give about 220 and 560,000, which the paper rounds to 200 and 10^6.

### Where Table 3 of the manuscript and the package differ

A few entries of the printed table do not agree with the exact computation. We list them so
that the table can be checked against the package output (all other entries, including the diagonal, the
`maxBF` row, and the nesting and dimension entries, agree):

* The overlaps of Model 10 with Models 2, 3, and 4 are printed as `.01`. Model 4 is nested in Model 10
  (the table itself says so in the lower triangle), so their overlap is Model 4 itself, with
  volume 1/720 = `r signif(1/720, 2)`. The overlaps with Models 2 and 3 are `r signif(cmp$volume["M2", "M10"], 2)`
  and `r signif(cmp$volume["M3", "M10"], 2)`.
* Row 6 (Model 6), column 1 (Model 1) is printed as "nested in", but Model 6 is not a subset of Model 1; their overlap
  is 5-dimensional.
* Row 7 (Model 7), column 6 (Model 6): the package finds that Model 7 contains Model 6 (relaxing an equality can only add
  points), the printed table shows a 5-dimensional overlap. Row 10, column 3 is printed as
  5-dimensional, but the overlap of Models 3 and 10 has positive volume, so it is 6-dimensional.

```{r table3-checks}
c(M6_in_M1 = fairy_nested(m$M6, m$M1), M6_in_M7 = fairy_nested(m$M6, m$M7),
  M3_M10_dim = fairy_dim(fairy_intersect(m$M3, m$M10)))
```

## Replication models (Table 4)

With r = 3 labs, each with six probabilities, replication models live in 18 dimensions.
`fairy_replicate()` builds the three versions of the paper:

* **identical**: every probability is the same in all labs, 12 equalities, dimension 6, volume zero.
* **joint**: each lab satisfies the model, labs are unrelated; the volume is the cube of the single-lab volume.
* **substitutable**: each constraint holds whichever lab's parameter is plugged in, for every term.

The columns of Table 4 are dimension, number of vertices, non-redundant inequalities, equalities,
and the upper bound on the Bayes factor:

```{r table4-m4}
rep_table <- function(h, r = 3, bf_substitutable = NULL) {
  ident <- fairy_info(fairy_replicate(h, r, "identical"))
  joint <- fairy_info(fairy_replicate(h, r, "joint"))
  subst <- fairy_info(fairy_replicate(h, r, "substitutable"), volume = FALSE)
  subst$max_bf <- if (is.null(bf_substitutable)) NA_real_ else bf_substitutable
  out <- rbind(identical = ident, joint = joint, substitutable = subst)
  out[, c("dim", "vertices", "inequalities", "equalities", "max_bf")]
}
```

For Model 4 the substitutable bound has a closed form: the 18 values fall into
six ordered groups of three, which happens with probability 3!^6 / 18!, so the bound is
`18! / 3!^6`. (For high-dimensional polytopes of this kind `fairy_volume(method = "volesti")` gives a stochastic estimate
if the volesti package is installed.)

```{r table4-m4-run}
exact_sub <- factorial(18) / factorial(3)^6
rep_table(m$M4, bf_substitutable = exact_sub)
format(exact_sub, scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)      # 1.37e11 in the paper
format(720^3, scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)          # "720^3 = 4e8" in the paper
```

Model 9 gives the same numbers:

```{r table4-m9}
rep_table(m$M9, bf_substitutable = exact_sub)
```

For the mixture model (Model 10) the joint model has 1,728 = 12^3 vertices and 3 x 64 = 192 inequalities,
and a bound of about 23^3 = 10^4:

```{r table4-m10}
joint10 <- fairy_info(fairy_replicate(m$M10, 3, "joint"))
joint10[, c("dim", "vertices", "inequalities", "equalities", "max_bf")]
fairy_info(fairy_replicate(m$M10, 3, "identical"), volume = FALSE)[, 1:4]
```

The substitutable version of Model 10 has 4,032 constraints. Removing redundant constraints in 18 dimensions takes
several minutes, so the vignette shows the constraint count before that step (`reduce = FALSE`),
which already equals the paper's number of non-redundant inequalities:

```{r table4-m10-sub}
nrow(fairy_replicate(m$M10, 3, "substitutable", reduce = FALSE))
```

To get the full row, including the 46,739 vertices, call
`fairy_info(fairy_replicate(m$M10, 3, "substitutable"), volume = FALSE)`; this takes a long time.

# Part 2: The Heuristic-Systematic Model (online supplement)

Here are the theoretical predictions of the supplement, again entered as constraint strings. In the 2 x 2 design the four
probabilities are `PbW, PbS, PsW, PsS` (`p1` to `p4`): big or small gap, weak or strong argument.
For the cue-congruence models the six probabilities `PiW, PnW, PcW, PiS, PnS, PcS` are `p1` to `p6`.

```{r hsm}
hsm <- lapply(c(
  pred1    = "p1 < p2; p3 < p4",                                  # stronger arguments never hurt
  pred2    = "p1 < p3; p2 < p4",                                  # a smaller gap never hurts
  pred3    = "p1 < p2 < p4; p1 < p3 < p4",                        # both
  pred6    = "p1 < p2 < p3; p4 < p5 < p6; p7 < p8 < p9; p1 < p4 < p7; p2 < p5 < p8; p3 < p6 < p9",
  override = "p6 > p3 > p2 = p1; p6 > p4 = p5 > p2",
  tradeoff = "p6 > p3 > p2 > p1; p6 > p5 > p4 > p1; p5 > p2",
  ttb      = "p1 = 0; p4 = 0; p2 = 1; p5 = 1; p3 = 1; p6 = 1"    # take the best
), fairy_h)
hsm$override_ttb_mixture <- fairy_mixture(hsm$override, hsm$ttb)
lab4 <- c("big, weak", "big, strong", "small, weak", "small, strong")
```

Prediction 1 says stronger arguments never reduce the share who act; prediction 2 says a smaller
gap never does. Each has nine extreme cases (Tables A1 and A2) and takes up a quarter of the
cube:

```{r hsm-a1}
fairy_words(hsm$pred1, labels = lab4)    # Table A1
fairy_words(hsm$pred2, labels = lab4)    # Table A2
sapply(hsm[c("pred1", "pred2")], fairy_max_bf)
```

Their combination, Prediction 3, has six extreme cases (Table A3), a volume of 1/12 and a largest Bayes factor of 12:

```{r hsm-a3}
fairy_words(hsm$pred3, labels = lab4)    # Table A3
fairy_info(hsm$pred3)
```

All six are vertices of both predictions, so intersecting the predictions adds no new extreme case:

```{r hsm-intersect}
fairy_nested(hsm$pred3, hsm$pred1) && fairy_nested(hsm$pred3, hsm$pred2)
```

## Two populations

If Prediction 3 must hold jointly in two populations, the bound is `12^2 = 144`. If it holds with
substitutable parameters, it is 420:

```{r hsm-replicate}
c(joint = fairy_max_bf(fairy_replicate(hsm$pred3, 2, "joint")),
  substitutable = fairy_max_bf(fairy_replicate(hsm$pred3, 2, "substitutable")))
```

## A 3-by-3 design

Three gap sizes and three argument strengths give nine probabilities. The twelve non-redundant order
constraints of equation (6) plus two range constraints give a bound of about 8,600 (8,640), about
60 times the bound 144 of the two-population replication:

```{r hsm-3x3}
fairy_info(hsm$pred6)
fairy_max_bf(hsm$pred6) / 144
```

## Cue congruence: Override, Trade-off, and take-the-best

The six probabilities are `PiW, PnW, PcW, PiS, PnS, PcS` (incongruent, no, or congruent cues; weak or strong
arguments). The Override Model (equation 7) contains two equalities and so has volume zero. Table A4 (top) lists its six extreme cases;
take-the-best (bottom) is a single point:

```{r hsm-a4}
lab6 <- c("inc, weak", "no, weak", "con, weak", "inc, strong", "no, strong", "con, strong")
fairy_words(hsm$override, labels = lab6)       # Table A4, top
fairy_words(hsm$ttb, labels = lab6)            # Table A4, bottom
fairy_info(hsm$override)[, c("dim", "vertices", "volume", "max_bf")]
```

The Trade-off Model (equation 8) has 10 vertices and a bound of 144. The Override Model is nested in it, but take-the-best
violates the Override Model:

```{r hsm-tradeoff}
fairy_info(hsm$tradeoff)[, c("dim", "vertices", "max_bf")]
c(override_in_tradeoff = fairy_nested(hsm$override, hsm$tradeoff),
  tradeoff_in_override = fairy_nested(hsm$tradeoff, hsm$override),
  ttb_in_override = fairy_nested(hsm$ttb, hsm$override))
```

Finally, the mixture of the Override Model and take-the-best adds the one vertex "none, all, all, none, all, all". It
keeps one equality (`PnW + PiS = PiW + PnS`), so its volume is zero and there is no upper bound on the Bayes factor. Both
components are nested in it (equation 10):

```{r hsm-mixture}
mixture <- hsm$override_ttb_mixture
fairy_constraints(mixture, labels = c("PiW", "PnW", "PcW", "PiS", "PnS", "PcS"))
c(override_nested = fairy_nested(hsm$override, mixture), ttb_nested = fairy_nested(hsm$ttb, mixture))
fairy_info(mixture)[, c("dim", "vertices", "inequalities", "equalities", "max_bf")]
```
